1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	Ambiguous policy clauses increase agent safety violations by 34.0\,pp (OR\,$=$\,15.1); clause-level wording drives 22.4\% of variance versus 0.4\% for type and 1.0\% for model (60.8\% residual). Effects range from $+$18.7\,pp (coreferential) to $+$36.0\,pp (authorization scope) among confound-controlled types, with incompleteness reaching $+$49.2\,pp (upper bound, conditional on an information-addition confound), forming a margin-dependent gradient across seven models. With disambiguation neglect in $>$89\% of cases and 41.3\% model-convergent violations, type-aware auditing and externalized detection are critical for customer-service deployments.

\paragraph{Prompt-based mitigation.}
Building on the five-model type-specific mitigation study ($-$8.5\,pp pooled, unpaired design; Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation}), we test whether disambiguation can be prompted at finer granularity using a matched-pair design. We evaluate generic awareness prompting (``the policy may contain ambiguous clauses; ask for clarification'') and type-specific prompting (targeting incompleteness, authorization scope, and lexical ambiguity individually) on GPT-5.4 with matched-pair McNemar tests ($n = 50$ per type). Generic prompting produces no overall reduction ($\Delta = +1.3$\,pp, $p > 0.5$). Type-specific results are asymmetric: authorization scope shows a marginal reduction ($-12$\,pp, $p = 0.070$), lexical ambiguity is unchanged ($-2$\,pp), and incompleteness \emph{worsens} ($+14$\,pp, $p = 0.118$; non-significant trend)---suggesting that prompting agents to attend to missing information may trigger confabulation rather than caution. The five-model study in Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation} uses a different prompt formulation and unpaired design, yielding directionally different results; mitigation outcomes appear sensitive to prompt wording and experimental design. That identical types show opposite directions under different prompt formulations (e.g., incompleteness: $-$3.4\,pp in v1 vs.\ $+$14\,pp in v2) underscores prompt sensitivity as a finding in itself, reinforcing the need for policy-design-level solutions rather than prompt-level fixes.

1	\section{Error Analysis \emph{[Exploratory]}}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	The following failure mode taxonomy emerges empirically from LLM-coded traces, distinct from the input ambiguity taxonomy (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
5	
6	We analyze 614 violation traces across all five models, coded into five failure modes: unauthorized escalation, assumption-based action, scope misapplication, arbitrary rule selection, and conservative refusal. GPT-5.4 and GPT-4.1 serve as detailed annotation anchors because they span the judge boundary. Inter-coder reliability is substantial (Gwet's AC$_1$ $= 0.62$ \citep{gwet_2014}; Cohen's $\kappa = 0.52$ \citep{cohen_1960}). The gap reflects the prevalence paradox: three categories account for ${\sim}$90\% of instances, compressing the $\kappa$ denominator and yielding artificially low values despite high raw agreement. Using LLMs to code LLM failure modes introduces a circularity risk that the moderate $\kappa$ may partly reflect; human-coded validation of at least one failure category would strengthen these findings.
7	
8	\subsection{Type-Specific Failure Mechanisms}
9	
10	The five-model data reveal three mechanistically distinct failure patterns that crosscut the specification/linguistic layer boundary.
11	
12	\emph{Structural misparse} (scope misapplication): the agent constructs an incorrect parse and follows it consistently, paralleling garden-path processing \citep{frazier_rayner_1982,ferreira_good_enough_2002} at a behavioral (not mechanistic) level---e.g., parsing ``items purchased with a coupon or during a sale are final'' as restricting only coupon purchases. This dominates scopal (all 5 models), conditional precedence (all 5), and coreferential (3/5).
13	
14	\emph{Information gap-filling} (assumption-based action): the agent fills missing information with plausible but incorrect defaults---e.g., inventing a 30-day return window when none is specified. This dominates incompleteness (3/5) and lexical (3/5).

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A customer asks to return a customized item within the 30-day window. The agent consults the store policy, which states that ``items may be returned within 30 days.'' The word ``items'' scopes over all product categories, including custom orders that are normally final sale. The agent grants a full refund and arranges free return shipping. One word of scopal ambiguity costs the retailer \$200.
5	
6	LLM-based agents increasingly operate under natural-language policy specifications that govern their permitted actions. These specifications inevitably contain ambiguity: a property that has been studied for decades in requirements engineering (RE) and computational linguistics. \citet{berry_kamsties_2004} distinguish between \emph{nocuous} (i.e., harmful) ambiguity, where different stakeholders arrive at different interpretations, and \emph{innocuous} ambiguity, where shared organizational context ensures convergent interpretation. In human RE workflows, most ambiguity is innocuous because developers share domain knowledge, can consult colleagues, and iteratively clarify requirements.
7	
8	LLM agents lack these disambiguation channels. They cannot consult colleagues, rarely escalate to users, and must resolve ambiguity in real time from the text alone. This raises a question that has not been empirically addressed: does policy ambiguity cause safety violations in LLM agents, and if so, does the \emph{type} of ambiguity predict the severity of the violation? Prior work classifies ambiguity types in policies \citep{drip_r_2026,li_ambiguity_taxonomy_2024} or measures policy understanding quality \citep{policybank_2026}, but no existing study provides a causal, type-granularity mapping from ambiguity to safety violations.

tool_args.old_string: Type membership explains only 0.4\% of violation variance versus 22.4\% for individual clause wording, because type differences manifest only under ambiguous conditions (all types produce $\sim$7\% violations when unambiguous). However, the taxonomy's value lies not in predicting violation rates but in predicting failure \emph{mechanisms}: each type maps to a mechanistically distinct failure pattern with cross-model consistency (\S\ref{sec:analysis}). Structural misparse dominates scopal and conditional precedence types (5/5 models each), information gap-filling dominates incompleteness and lexical types ($\geq$3/5), and boundary violation dominates authorization scope exclusively (5/5, with zero conservative refusals). This near-deterministic type$\to$mechanism mapping enables targeted intervention design---parse constraints for structural misparse, information supplementation for gap-filling, boundary enforcement for authorization scope---even though type membership is a poor predictor of individual clause risk.

4	\paragraph{Scope.} We evaluate seven API-accessible models from six providers (Appendix~\ref{app:model_expansion}); smaller open-source models (7B--70B) may exhibit different vulnerability patterns. $\tau^2$-bench covers retail and airline customer service only---effects in other domains remain untested, though within-study cross-domain consistency is encouraging. Our matched-pair design requires synthetic ambiguity construction, which may not capture the full distribution of naturally occurring ambiguities; realism validation (\S\ref{sec:method}) confirms lexical comparability but cannot rule out distributional gaps. Coreferential ambiguity was excluded from mitigation and replication experiments due to benchmark-specific structural constraints (Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation}).
5	
6	\paragraph{Measurement.} Each model is evaluated by a single cross-judge, confounding judge identity with model identity; within-judge-group analyses confirm C1 individually (both $p < 0.001$) but not C3 (Appendix~\ref{app:judge_group_ranking}), and cross-model type ranking concordance is only moderate (Appendix~\ref{app:kendall_w}). Most critically, cross-judge-group type rankings show near-zero correlation ($\rho = 0.09$, $p = 0.87$; Appendix~\ref{app:judge_group_ranking}), meaning that the C2 gradient's mid-tier ordering does not generalize across judge groups---though excluding authorization scope yields strong concordance ($\rho = 0.90$, $p = 0.037$), and incompleteness as the highest-risk type is robust to this variation.
